topic: Late-onset (adult-onset) ADHD
claim: Follow-up studies find most 'late' cases began in adolescence or had earlier signs, and true adult onset is rare or unproven ('the current consensus is mostly adolescent onset, or missed').

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Several population birth cohorts found that most young adults meeting ADHD criteria had not met criteria in childhood (Dunedin 90%; E-Risk 67.5% of 166; Pelotas only 12.6% had childhood ADHD), with comparable impairment, leading authors to propose late onset as real and possibly a distinct syndrome.

sources.citation: Moffitt TE, et al. Is adult ADHD a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder? Evidence from a four-decade longitudinal cohort study. Am J Psychiatry. 2015.
Agnew-Blais JC, et al. Evaluation of the persistence, remission, and emergence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in young adulthood. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.
Caye A, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder trajectories from childhood to young adulthood: evidence from a birth cohort supporting a late-onset syndrome. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: With repeated, multi-informant assessment, about 95% of apparent late cases were excluded (substance use, other conditions), remaining cases began in adolescence; a cohort analysis found parent-rated late-onset ADHD resembled child-onset ADHD in polygenic risk and cognition, suggesting delayed emergence (perhaps due to childhood resources) rather than a different disorder.

sources.citation: Sibley MH, et al. Late-onset ADHD reconsidered with comprehensive repeated assessments between ages 10 and 25. Am J Psychiatry. 2018.
Asherson P, et al. Annual Research Review: Does late-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder exist? J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2019.
Riglin L, et al. "Late-onset" ADHD symptoms in young adulthood: is this ADHD? J Atten Disord. 2022.

why_they_may_differ: Cohorts that measured ADHD at few time points, with screening tools, single informants or self-report in adulthood (Dunedin, E-Risk, Pelotas) find much more 'late onset'; studies with dense repeated assessments and exclusion of substance use and other disorders (MTA comparison group) find little. Self-report versus parent report changes the picture (Riglin). The Pelotas childhood screen used a questionnaire subscale. Samples also differ in country and era.
next_step: Add the E-Risk and Pelotas cohorts (and Riglin 2022) so the page shows that three of four large population cohorts found large late-onset groups; tabulate each cohort by assessment density, informant and exclusion rules to show how method drives the estimate; consider softening 'current consensus' to 'the leading interpretation'.

topic: Is the rise filling a gap or overdiagnosis?
claim: The same system over-diagnoses some groups (young-for-year, milder cases) and under-diagnoses others (older adults, minority children, girls).

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Evidence consistent with overdiagnosis in children: rising diagnosis and prescribing, extra cases tending to be milder, and a few studies suggesting diminishing returns where harms may outweigh benefits for mild cases.

sources.citation: Kazda L, et al. Overdiagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: a systematic scoping review. JAMA Netw Open. 2021.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Recorded ADHD in England in 2025 (1.19% of patients) was still well below expected prevalence in every age group, from about 29% shortfall in young men to about 94% in people over 65, read by the authors as continued under-recognition. A 2026 multi-author UK commentary concluded there is no evidence of UK overdiagnosis (while noting rigorous post-pandemic data are lacking and some low-quality assessments may misdiagnose), and an editorial by the chair of the NHS-England ADHD taskforce noted UK administrative prevalence is below population rates.

sources.citation: John A, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children and adults in England, 2000-2025: recorded prevalence and diagnostic trends. Lancet Reg Health Eur. 2026.
Cortese S, et al. ADHD (over) diagnosis: fiction, fashion and failure. Br J Psychiatry. 2026.
Thapar A. Editorial Perspective: Overdiagnosis of ADHD? Here we go again. Child Adolesc Ment Health. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: Kazda's evidence is mostly from children and from high-diagnosing systems (US, Australia) before 2020; John compares coded GP diagnoses in England against prevalence benchmarks from other studies, and GP coding may miss specialist or private diagnoses (understating recorded prevalence). 'Milder' new cases can be read either as overdiagnosis or as legitimate diagnoses of a dimensional condition. Both may be true in different groups.
next_step: Add the 2026 UK commentaries (Cortese; Thapar) so the page shows the current UK expert position as well as Kazda; weigh against direct outcome evidence: find studies comparing outcomes (benefit and harm) of diagnosis/treatment in near-threshold cases; check whether John et al. adjust for private-sector diagnoses not coded in GP records; add any newer overdiagnosis/underdiagnosis estimates for adults.

topic: Twin heritability versus measured DNA and indirect genetic effects
claim: About 74% of variation in ADHD is genetic (twin studies); 'about a third' of heritability comes from common variants; ADHD runs in families 'mostly through genes'.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Pooled twin studies give heritability of about 74%; a Swedish clinical-diagnosis twin register gives 0.88 overall and 0.72 in adults; family clustering tracks genetic relatedness.

sources.citation: Faraone SV, et al. Genetics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Mol Psychiatry. 2019.
Larsson H, et al. The heritability of clinically diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder across the lifespan. Psychol Med. 2014.
Chen Q, et al. Familial aggregation of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2017.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Measured common DNA explains much less; in Norwegian parent-offspring trios, genetic effects acting through parents (indirect genetic effects, i.e. the family environment parents' genes create) explained more variance than the child's own (direct) genes for hyperactivity at age 3 (9.6% versus 1.3%) and inattention (6.7% versus 4.8%).

sources.citation: Hegemann L, et al. Direct and indirect genetic effects on early neurodevelopmental traits. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: Twin designs assume equal environments for identical and non-identical twins and can be inflated by rater contrast effects in parent ratings; SNP-based methods capture only common variants and are confounded by indirect effects and population structure, which within-family designs remove. The 'about a third' figure is from a 2019 review summarising earlier GWAS; the 2023 GWAS's own SNP-heritability figure was not confirmed from its abstract for this register. Hegemann measured mother-rated traits at age 3, not diagnosed ADHD.
next_step: Confirm the SNP heritability reported in the full text of Demontis 2023 (DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01285-8) and update 'about a third' if it is lower; add within-family/trio evidence on indirect genetic effects to the 'missing heritability' bullet; soften 'mostly through genes' on what-adhd-is.md to make clear heritability includes gene-environment interplay.

topic: After giving birth: is the evidence only two uncontrolled surveys?
claim: After giving birth the evidence is two surveys of women with ADHD, neither with a comparison group.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: The page's sources: a Dutch clinic survey (57.6% above a postnatal depression cut-off) and a 2026 online survey (70% reported worsening), both without comparison groups and both relying on recall.

sources.citation: Dorani F, et al. Prevalence of hormone-related mood disorder symptoms in women with ADHD. J Psychiatr Res. 2021.
Osianlis E, et al. ADHD in females: survey findings on symptoms across hormonal life stages. J Psychiatr Res. 2026.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Controlled studies now exist. In Ontario health records (about 1.05 million pregnancies), perinatal mental illness was diagnosed in 50.2% of those with ADHD against 24.0% without (adjusted relative risk 1.35; perinatal depression 14.4% against 5.0%). A Canadian national survey found mothers with possible ADHD had about 1.7 times the odds of postpartum depression and anxiety.

sources.citation: Vigod SN, et al. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and perinatal mental illness: a population-based study. Soc Psychiatry Psychiatr Epidemiol. 2026.

Johnson D, et al. Associations between self-reported ADHD symptoms and depression and anxiety in mothers and fathers during the postpartum period: A Canadian nationwide longitudinal study. J Affect Disord. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: The page's statement reflects its own source set, not the field. The newer studies measure perinatal mental illness (largely depression and anxiety) rather than whether ADHD symptoms themselves worsen, so they answer a related but different question. Health-record diagnoses miss untreated cases but avoid recall bias; women with ADHD may also be more often in contact with services and so more often diagnosed.
next_step: Update the 'After giving birth' bullet and short answer: large controlled data (Vigod 2026, with absolute figures) show raised perinatal depression and anxiety in women with ADHD, while whether ADHD symptoms themselves worsen still rests on uncontrolled surveys. Keep the help-now link next to the perinatal depression figures. Cross-check with 06-treatment-what-works/pregnancy-and-breastfeeding.md.

topic: Dementia risk
claim: Dementia: a real registry link, much weaker than headlines suggest; it weakens considerably after accounting for other psychiatric conditions (Swedish HR 2.92 to 1.62), and a 2023 review judged evidence too varied to combine.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Weaker or confounded: in 3.6 million Swedes, the hazard ratio fell from 2.92 to 1.62 after accounting for depression, anxiety, substance use and bipolar disorder; part of the link runs in families; reverse causation (early dementia mislabelled as ADHD) is possible; a 2023 systematic review could not pool studies.

sources.citation: Dobrosavljevic M, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder as a risk factor for dementia and mild cognitive impairment: a population-based register study. Eur Psychiatry. 2022.
Becker S, et al. Risk of neurodegenerative disease or dementia in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review. Front Psychiatry. 2023.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Newer evidence points to a sizeable, partly genetic link: a 2026 meta-analysis of five studies pooled a hazard ratio of 2.52 for all-cause dementia; in 187,341 US adults aged 50+ (All of Us), cognitive impairment developed in 6.7% with ADHD against 3.4% without (HR 4.60, attenuated but not removed by adjustment), and a higher ADHD polygenic score also predicted impairment (HR 1.35), as it did in a separate multicohort study (10-year incidence 33.8% against 23.4% by score tertile).

sources.citation: Levine SZ, et al. Adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and the risk of dementia. JAMA Netw Open. 2023.
Baiamonte L, et al. Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Risk of Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Brain Sci. 2026.
Bauer-Negrini G, et al. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Late-Life Cognitive Impairment. JAMA Psychiatry. 2026.
sources.design: cohort with EHR and polygenic scores (All of Us)

sources.citation: Leffa DT, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder polygenic risk score and incidence of cognitive impairment in older adults: A prospective multicohort study. Alzheimers Dement. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: Studies differ in whether they adjust for psychiatric conditions that may lie on the pathway, in the outcome (dementia versus the broader 'cognitive impairment'), and in how ADHD is identified late in life, where new attention complaints can be early dementia (reverse causation). Polygenic-score links are less prone to reverse causation but can reflect shared genetics with education, vascular risk or psychiatric illness; the meta-analysis pooled only five studies, likely including the Swedish and Israeli ones already cited, so it does not add independent data so much as summarise them.
next_step: Revisit the heading 'much weaker than headlines suggest': it remains fair for the Swedish adjusted estimate but sits awkwardly beside a 2026 pooled HR of 2.52 and the All of Us HR of 4.60 with genetic support. Add the 2026 meta-analysis and All of Us study with absolute figures (6.7% against 3.4% over about 10 years), keep the reverse-causation and confounding caveats, and note that 'cognitive impairment' includes mild cognitive impairment, not only dementia. Check overlap of studies in the meta-analysis before treating it as independent.

topic: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) in pregnancy
claim: Paracetamol in pregnancy does not appear to cause ADHD; there is no link once families are accounted for.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Sibling-comparison studies and reviews that weight them find the small whole-population association disappears within families, pointing to shared family factors (for example the mother's own genes or the illnesses that lead to taking paracetamol).

sources.citation: Ahlqvist VH, et al. Acetaminophen use during pregnancy and children's risk of autism, ADHD, and intellectual disability. JAMA. 2024.

Sheikh J, et al. Maternal paracetamol (acetaminophen) use during pregnancy and risk of autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in offspring: umbrella review of systematic reviews. BMJ. 2025.
Gustavson K, et al. Acetaminophen use during pregnancy and offspring attention deficit hyperactivity disorder - a longitudinal sibling control study. JCPP Adv. 2021.
Okubo Y, et al. Maternal Acetaminophen Use and Offspring's Neurodevelopmental Outcome: A Nationwide Birth Cohort Study. Paediatr Perinat Epidemiol. 2026.
sources.design: nationwide administrative birth cohort (Japan) with sibling comparison, bias analysis and negative controls

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Some reviews and biomarker studies read the evidence as consistent with a real effect, especially for long or heavy use, and argue sibling designs can hide true effects. A Navigation Guide review of 46 studies concluded the evidence supports an association and called for limiting use; a cord-blood study found a dose-response pattern; the Norwegian study found long-term use (29+ days) doubled risk between families before the sibling analysis removed it.

sources.citation: Prada D, et al. Evaluation of the evidence on acetaminophen use and neurodevelopmental disorders using the Navigation Guide methodology. Environ Health. 2025.

Ji Y, et al. Association of Cord Plasma Biomarkers of In Utero Acetaminophen Exposure With Risk of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Autism Spectrum Disorder in Childhood. JAMA Psychiatry. 2020.
sources.design: prospective cohort with cord-plasma biomarkers (Boston Birth Cohort)

why_they_may_differ: Side B relies mainly on whole-population comparisons, which cannot separate paracetamol from the reasons for taking it (fever, infection, pain) or from the mother's genes; the cord-blood study measured exposure well but was a small, high-risk clinic sample with little control for family factors. Side A's sibling designs remove fixed family factors but lose precision, depend on mothers whose use differed between pregnancies, and are biased towards no effect when exposure is misrecorded, which Prada and colleagues argue can hide a small or dose-dependent effect. The Japanese study's bias analyses suggested misclassification and confounding inflate, rather than hide, the observed link.
next_step: Add one sentence acknowledging that a 2025 Navigation Guide review (Prada et al.) reached the opposite reading and why it differs (no sibling weighting, qualitative synthesis), and consider citing the Norwegian and Japanese sibling studies as independent replications of the Swedish null. Check whether long-duration use has been tested specifically in sibling designs beyond Gustavson 2021, and soften 'no link' to 'no link within families' in the heading if long-term-use data stay thin.

topic: Certainty of methylphenidate evidence in children (Cochrane vs umbrella/network reviews)
claim: Reviews agree on the short-term size of methylphenidate's effect in children (SMD about 0.74-0.78) but disagree on its certainty: Cochrane rates it very low, the 2025 BMJ umbrella review moderate or high.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Cochrane finds a teacher-rated SMD of 0.74 but judges almost every trial at high risk of bias (unblinding through side effects, industry funding), so rates all outcomes very low certainty. Its authors defended these judgements against critics.

sources.citation: Storebø OJ, et al. Methylphenidate for children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2025 (CD009885.pub4).
Storebø OJ, et al. Response to "Trust, but verify" by Banaschewski et al. Z Kinder Jugendpsychiatr Psychother. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Network and umbrella reviews find the same or slightly larger effect and grade it moderate to high certainty; the European ADHD Guidelines Group argued Cochrane's risk-of-bias calls were too severe and that high- and low-risk trials gave similar results.

sources.citation: Gosling CJ, et al. Benefits and harms of ADHD interventions: umbrella review and platform for shared decision making. BMJ. 2025;391:e085875.

Cortese S, et al. Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for ADHD in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Lancet Psychiatry. 2018;5(9):727-38.
Banaschewski T, et al. Methylphenidate for ADHD in children and adolescents: throwing the baby out with the bathwater. Evid Based Ment Health. 2016.

why_they_may_differ: Both sides use GRADE, but GRADE needs judgement at the risk-of-bias step. Cochrane treats possible unblinding through side effects and industry funding as high risk and marks the whole body of evidence down; the other groups weigh the fact that high- and low-risk trials give similar results and do not mark down as far. The numbers barely differ; the confidence label does.
next_step: Cite the Cochrane authors' 2016 reply (PMID 27658627) so both sides are represented by primary text, and tabulate the risk-of-bias decisions of each review side by side for the same trials, including any sensitivity analysis restricted to low-risk trials in the 2025 Cochrane update.

topic: Does medication improve quality of life in adults?
claim: In adults, symptom relief did not bring measurable quality-of-life gains; medicines were not efficacious on quality of life.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: A 2025 component network meta-analysis of 113 adult trials found medicines reduced core symptoms but were not efficacious on other outcomes such as quality of life; a withdrawal-trial meta-analysis found a quality-of-life drop after stopping only in children.

sources.citation: Ostinelli EG, et al. Comparative efficacy and acceptability of pharmacological, psychological, and neurostimulatory interventions for ADHD in adults: a systematic review and component network meta-analysis. Lancet Psychiatry. 2025;12(1):32-43.

Tsujii N, et al. Effect of continuing and discontinuing medications on quality of life after symptomatic remission in ADHD: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;81(3):19r13015.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 17 placebo-controlled RCTs (5,388 people) found amphetamines (g 0.51), methylphenidate (0.38) and atomoxetine (0.30) improved quality of life more than placebo; for atomoxetine the effect did not differ between children and adults.

sources.citation: Bellato A, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis: effects of pharmacological treatment for ADHD on quality of life. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: Different trial sets, quality-of-life scales and analytic models: Ostinelli's component network model across many interventions may have had few quality-of-life data points per comparison and wide intervals, while Bellato pooled placebo-controlled medication trials directly. Effects in Bellato are smaller than for symptoms and quality of life is often self-rated by participants who may guess their allocation. The abstract does not split stimulant effects by age, so the adult-specific stimulant estimate needs the full text.
next_step: Add Bellato 2025 and change the short answer from 'did not bring measurable quality-of-life gains' to 'evidence on quality of life is mixed: one large adult network analysis found no clear benefit, while a meta-analysis of 17 trials found small-to-moderate gains'. Extract adult-only estimates from Bellato's full text. Also update the matching sentence on 07/when-your-partner-has-adhd.md.

topic: How often psychosis or mania follows stimulant treatment
claim: Psychosis is rare: about 1 in 660 young people starting a stimulant (0.10% methylphenidate, 0.21% amphetamine) developed new psychosis treated with an antipsychotic.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: US insurance and hospital case-control data put new psychosis at about 1 to 2 per 1,000 starters, higher with amphetamine and with high amphetamine doses; methylphenidate was not linked in the case-control study.

sources.citation: Moran LV, et al. Psychosis with methylphenidate or amphetamine in patients with ADHD. N Engl J Med. 2019;380:1128-38.
Moran LV, et al. Risk of incident psychosis and mania with prescription amphetamines. Am J Psychiatry. 2024;181(10):901-9.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 16 studies (391,043 people) found 2.3% of stimulant-treated people developed a psychotic disorder, 2.8% psychotic symptoms and 3.7% bipolar disorder, about ten times the page's headline rate, with amphetamines worse than methylphenidate (OR 1.57).

sources.citation: Salazar de Pablo G, et al. Occurrence of psychosis and bipolar disorder in individuals with ADHD treated with stimulants: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2025.

positions.label: C
positions.summary: Within-person register studies find no rise in psychotic events after starting methylphenidate (IRR 1.04, even in people with past psychosis), and no rise in mania when methylphenidate is taken with a mood stabiliser, though mania rose sharply with methylphenidate alone in bipolar disorder (HR 6.7).

sources.citation: Hollis C, et al. Methylphenidate and the risk of psychosis in adolescents and young adults: a population-based cohort study. Lancet Psychiatry. 2019.
Viktorin A, et al. The risk of treatment-emergent mania with methylphenidate in bipolar disorder. Am J Psychiatry. 2017.

why_they_may_differ: They measure different things. The US cohort counts new psychosis serious enough for antipsychotic treatment in a fixed window; the meta-analysis pools any psychotic symptoms over long and variable follow-up, has no unexposed comparison group, and is very heterogeneous (I2 above 95%), with higher rates in small, North American and long-follow-up studies. Within-person designs ask whether risk rises after starting compared with before, which removes background risk that people with ADHD already carry.
next_step: Add the 2025 meta-analysis and the Swedish within-person studies, separate 'how many treated people ever develop psychosis' (prevalence, no comparator) from 'does starting medication raise risk' (comparative), and state that the 1-in-660 figure is a short-window incidence in US 13-25-year-olds. Mention the bipolar/mood-stabiliser finding as a reported study result, without advice.

topic: Long-term benefit: withdrawal trials vs naturalistic MTA follow-up
claim: After two years methylphenidate still helped children on average (40% vs 16% worsened on placebo), while in the MTA follow-up early differences faded and extended use was not linked to fewer adult symptoms.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Randomised discontinuation trials show more worsening after switching to placebo in children treated for over two years and in adults stable on lisdexamfetamine (75% vs 9% relapse).

sources.citation: Matthijssen AM, et al. Continued benefits of methylphenidate in ADHD after 2 years in clinical practice: a randomized placebo-controlled discontinuation study. Am J Psychiatry. 2019;176(9):754-62.
Brams M, et al. Maintenance of efficacy of lisdexamfetamine dimesylate in adults with ADHD: randomized withdrawal design. J Clin Psychiatry. 2012;73(7):977-83.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: In the MTA, original group differences were gone by 3 years; by 8 years medication in the previous year was not linked to better functioning, and at 16 years consistent use was linked to shorter height but not fewer symptoms.

sources.citation: Molina BSG, et al. The MTA at 8 years: prospective follow-up of children treated for combined-type ADHD in a multisite study. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2009;48(5):484-500.
Swanson JM, et al. Young adult outcomes in the follow-up of the multimodal treatment study of ADHD. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2017;58(6):663-78.

why_they_may_differ: Withdrawal trials enrol people who already respond and tolerate the drug (enriched), run for weeks, and can mistake rebound or unblinding for relapse. The MTA follow-up is non-randomised after 14 months, so families of more impaired children may have kept medicating (confounding by indication), which hides benefit. They answer different questions: 'does it still work for current responders now' vs 'does a childhood treatment strategy change the adult course'.
next_step: Keep both, and add a one-line explanation that the designs answer different questions; consider adding the 2025 target-trial emulations (Zhang 2025, Li 2024) as a third, intermediate design for longer-term outcomes.

topic: Size of registry benefits: within-person designs vs target-trial emulation
claim: During medicated periods the same people had roughly a third fewer criminal convictions, crash-related emergency visits and substance-related emergencies; injuries were also less common.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Within-person register and claims studies find reductions of about 30-40% in convictions, crash emergencies and substance-related emergencies during medicated periods, and a protective effect on injuries in self-controlled studies.

sources.citation: Lichtenstein P, et al. Medication for attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder and criminality. N Engl J Med. 2012;367:2006-14.
Chang Z, et al. Association between medication use for ADHD and risk of motor vehicle crashes. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017;74(6):597-603.
Quinn PD, et al. ADHD medication and substance-related problems. Am J Psychiatry. 2017;174(9):877-85.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A 2025 Swedish target-trial emulation (148,581 people) comparing starting vs not starting medication found smaller first-event reductions: suicidal behaviour 17%, substance misuse 15%, transport accidents 12%, criminality 13%, and no clear reduction in accidental injuries (IRR 0.98). It also reports absolute rates, e.g. criminality 65.1 vs 76.1 per 1,000 person-years.

sources.citation: Zhang L, et al. ADHD drug treatment and risk of suicidal behaviours, substance misuse, accidental injuries, transport accidents, and criminality: emulation of target trials. BMJ. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: Within-person designs compare on- and off-medication months, so time-varying factors (crises before starting, stopping during chaotic periods) can enlarge the apparent benefit; they also answer a different question (being on vs off at a given time). Target-trial emulation compares people who start with similar people who do not, over a fixed period, using an intention-to-treat style analysis that dilutes effects when people stop. The newer design suggests the same direction with smaller effects and, for first injuries, no clear effect.
next_step: Add the 2025 target-trial emulation with its absolute rates per 1,000 person-years, which fills the page's stated gap on absolute numbers; soften 'injuries were also less common' to note that the newest design found no clear reduction in first injuries (recurrent injuries fell slightly, IRR 0.96).

topic: How often childhood ADHD persists into adulthood
claim: About 15% still meet full criteria at 25 (65% counting partial remission); most MTA participants fluctuate; other cohorts find fluctuation less often.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Meta-analysis of older follow-up studies: about 15% persist with full criteria at age 25, about 65% if impairing subthreshold symptoms are counted.

sources.citation: Faraone SV, et al. The age-dependent decline of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis of follow-up studies. Psychol Med. 2006.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: In the MTA cohort (8 assessments to age 25) 63.8% fluctuated in and out of threshold and only 9.1% fully recovered; three other US cohorts found fluctuation in 17-29% and never as the largest group.

sources.citation: Sibley MH, et al. Variable patterns of remission from ADHD in the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD. Am J Psychiatry. 2022.
Norman LJ, et al. Longitudinal trajectories of childhood and adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnoses in three cohorts. EClinicalMedicine. 2023.

why_they_may_differ: Persistence rates depend on how many times people are assessed (more assessments reveal fluctuation), who reports (self versus parent), whether impairment and subthreshold symptoms count, and whether samples are clinic-referred (MTA) or population-based (ABCD). The Faraone figures pool older studies with mostly two time points.
next_step: Present persistence as a range conditioned on definition and number of assessments; check for a newer pooled persistence meta-analysis (post-2015) to update the 2006 figures.

topic: Ethnic differences: missed diagnoses or different measurement?
claim: Lower diagnosis rates in Asian, Black and Hispanic US children look partly like missed diagnoses; but a meta-analysis estimated higher ADHD prevalence in Black Americans.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Insurance-claims and survey cohorts found minority children less likely to be diagnosed and treated, interpreted as under-diagnosis of minority children rather than over-diagnosis of White children.

sources.citation: Shi Y, et al. Racial disparities in diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in a US national birth cohort. JAMA Netw Open. 2021.
Coker TR, et al. Racial and ethnic disparities in ADHD diagnosis and treatment. Pediatrics. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A meta-analysis of 21 US studies estimated ADHD at about 14.5% among Black individuals, higher than general US estimates.

sources.citation: Cénat JM, et al. Prevalence and risk factors associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder among US Black individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2021.

why_they_may_differ: A uses recorded diagnoses in insured populations; B pools symptom-based estimates, many from disadvantaged samples, where adversity raises symptom scores and rating scales may not be measurement-invariant across groups. Both can be true: higher symptom levels in some samples and lower access to diagnosis.
next_step: Look for measurement-invariance studies of ADHD rating scales across US ethnic groups, and for a non-US (UK/Australia) registry study of ethnicity and ADHD diagnosis, which the page says is missing.

topic: Stable prevalence versus rising diagnoses
claim: The share of children who meet ADHD criteria has not risen over three decades, while recorded diagnoses have risen sharply (US, Sweden, England).

positions.label: A
positions.summary: When standardised criteria are applied in community samples, the proportion of children meeting ADHD criteria is stable across decades and regions; in Swedish twins, diagnosis-level parent-rated symptoms did not change 2004-2014.

sources.citation: Polanczyk GV, et al. ADHD prevalence estimates across three decades: an updated systematic review and meta-regression analysis. Int J Epidemiol. 2014.

Rydell M, et al. Has the attention deficit hyperactivity disorder phenotype become more common in children between 2004 and 2014? Trends over 10 years from a Swedish general population sample. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2018.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Diagnosed ADHD has risen substantially: parent-reported US diagnoses from 6.1% to 10.2% (1997-2016), Swedish register diagnoses more than fivefold, and English GP-recorded new diagnoses accelerating after 2020.

sources.citation: Xu G, et al. Twenty-year trends in diagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder among US children and adolescents, 1997-2016. JAMA Netw Open. 2018.
John A, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children and adults in England, 2000-2025: recorded prevalence and diagnostic trends. Lancet Reg Health Eur. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: These are not strictly contradictory: A measures how many children meet criteria when everyone is assessed the same way; B measures who reaches a clinician and gets a recorded diagnosis. The gap is filled by changes in awareness, access, thresholds and recording. The open dispute is how much of the gap is catching previously missed cases versus adding milder or borderline ones. Polanczyk's series ends in about 2013, before the post-2020 surge, so 'stable true prevalence' is an extrapolation for the most recent period.
next_step: Look for community prevalence surveys using standardised criteria conducted after 2020 (for example, repeated national child mental-health surveys) to test whether true prevalence is still flat during the post-pandemic diagnosis surge; state on the page that the stable-prevalence series predates 2020.

topic: How common is ADHD in children: 5-8% or about 2.7%?
claim: Pooled studies put ADHD in roughly 5-8% of children and adolescents (WFADHD 5.9%; Salari 7.6% for ages 3-12 and 5.6% for 12-18).

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Meta-analyses of community studies give child/adolescent prevalence around 5-8%; Cortese's re-analysis of the GBD's own input data (pre-2013) gave 5.41%.

sources.citation: Faraone SV, et al. The World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement: 208 evidence-based conclusions about the disorder. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2021.
Salari N, et al. The global prevalence of ADHD in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ital J Pediatr. 2023.

Cortese S, et al. Incidence, prevalence, and global burden of ADHD from 1990 to 2019 across 204 countries: data, with critical re-analysis, from the Global Burden of Disease study. Mol Psychiatry. 2023.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: The Global Burden of Disease study, widely used in policy, modelled child/adolescent prevalence at 2.68% and lifespan prevalence at 1.13% in 2019, with a slight fall (-8.75%) in age-standardised prevalence since 1990.

sources.citation: Cortese S, et al. Incidence, prevalence, and global burden of ADHD from 1990 to 2019 across 204 countries: data, with critical re-analysis, from the Global Burden of Disease study. Mol Psychiatry. 2023.

why_they_may_differ: GBD imputes prevalence for countries with no data and applies its own case definitions, which Cortese et al. argue underestimate ADHD; meta-analyses pool heterogeneous surveys, often with screening tools that can overestimate (Salari's 7.6% is high). Readers will meet the GBD figure in news and policy documents, so the gap needs explaining.
next_step: Add one sentence on what-adhd-is.md noting the much lower GBD modelled estimate and why it differs; check whether GBD 2023 (Lancet 2026, PMID 42167272) revised the ADHD figure.

topic: Sex differences in symptom presentation
claim: On full clinical interviews, core symptom severity looks similar across sexes; separately, expert consensus says girls tend to present with more inattention and less disruptive behaviour.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: A 2024 meta-analysis of 52 studies found no significant sex difference in core symptom severity on clinical interviews, in children or adults.

sources.citation: Young S, et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the severity of core symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in females and males. Psychol Med. 2024.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Earlier meta-analyses of diagnosed youth found boys rated more hyperactive than girls (and, in the older review, girls rated lower on all symptom domains), with boys showing more motor-inhibition and flexibility difficulties; the expert consensus also describes a more inattentive, less disruptive female presentation.

sources.citation: Loyer Carbonneau M, et al. Meta-analysis of sex differences in ADHD symptoms and associated cognitive deficits. J Atten Disord. 2021.
Gershon J. A meta-analytic review of gender differences in ADHD. J Atten Disord. 2002.

Young S, et al. Females with ADHD: an expert consensus statement taking a lifespan approach providing guidance for the identification and treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in girls and women. BMC Psychiatry. 2020.

why_they_may_differ: Young 2024 restricted to clinical interviews, which may standardise ratings; the other meta-analyses pooled rating scales from parents and teachers, where rater expectation and referral bias (more severely hyperactive girls are referred) operate. 'No difference in severity among those diagnosed' and 'girls present differently in the population' can both be true because diagnosed girls are a selected group.
next_step: Add the Loyer Carbonneau 2021 meta-analysis (hyperactivity higher in boys) alongside Young 2024, and explain that diagnosed samples are selected; check whether Young 2024 analysed hyperactivity and inattention separately by measure.

topic: Does stimulant medication change brain structure?
claim: ENIGMA found no medication effect on subcortical volumes; smaller VBM meta-analyses linked stimulant use to more typical brain measures; 'no randomised trial has settled it'.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: In the largest mega-analysis (3,242 scans), subcortical differences were the same with or without stimulant history; a 1-year placebo-controlled trial in adults found no grey-matter volume loss with methylphenidate (a trend to cerebellar grey-matter increase).

sources.citation: Hoogman M, et al. Subcortical brain volume differences in participants with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adults: a cross-sectional mega-analysis. Lancet Psychiatry. 2017.
Tebartz van Elst L, et al. The effect of methylphenidate intake on brain structure in adults with ADHD in a placebo-controlled randomized trial. J Psychiatry Neurosci. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: VBM meta-analyses found samples with more stimulant-treated participants had more typical basal ganglia values; a 16-week randomised placebo-controlled trial found methylphenidate increased white-matter FA in several tracts in boys aged 10-12 but not in adult men, suggesting age-dependent medication effects.

sources.citation: Nakao T, et al. Gray matter volume abnormalities in ADHD: voxel-based meta-analysis exploring the effects of age and stimulant medication. Am J Psychiatry. 2011.
Frodl T, Skokauskas N. Meta-analysis of structural MRI studies in children and adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder indicates treatment effects. Acta Psychiatr Scand. 2012.
Bouziane C, et al. White matter by diffusion MRI following methylphenidate treatment: a randomized control trial in males with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Radiology. 2019.

why_they_may_differ: Cross-study associations (meta-regression on % medicated) are confounded by severity and age; ENIGMA's medication data are lifetime yes/no histories from mixed sites. The two trials are small, short and measure different things (grey-matter volume in adults versus white-matter FA in boys), and they actually agree that adults show little change; Bouziane's region-of-interest analysis was null and only a voxel-wise age interaction was significant.
next_step: Update the page's 'No randomised trial has settled it': add the two small RCTs (Tebartz van Elst 2016; Bouziane 2019) and explain they suggest possible age-dependent white-matter effects in children and no volume loss in adults, without settling long-term effects. Check for further ePOD-MPH outputs (grey matter, dopamine).

topic: "Three years behind": cortical maturation delay
claim: Half the cortex reached peak thickness about 3 years later in children with ADHD (Shaw 2007); ENIGMA found mostly no thickness differences.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: A longitudinal cohort found a delay in the age of peak cortical thickness (10.5 versus 7.5 years); a 2026 systematic review of 32 longitudinal MRI studies concluded that delayed peaks in thickness, surface area and gyrification are a recurring finding.

sources.citation: Shaw P, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is characterized by a delay in cortical maturation. PNAS. 2007.
Ishii-Takahashi A, et al. Longitudinal MRI studies of children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2026.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: The large ENIGMA cortical analysis found thickness differences in only two regions in children and none in adolescents or adults; the 2026 review's own meta-analysis found no difference in longitudinal change of total grey matter; an ABCD brain-age study found 'younger-looking' regional brain age in ADHD but tiny effects (d -0.08 to -0.12).

sources.citation: Hoogman M, et al. Brain imaging of the cortex in ADHD: a coordinated analysis of large-scale clinical and population-based samples. Am J Psychiatry. 2019.
Gagnon A, et al. Regional brain age deviations reveal divergent developmental pathways in youth. Biol Psychiatry Cogn Neurosci Neuroimaging. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: Shaw measured timing of a peak with repeated scans in one NIMH sample; ENIGMA compares thickness at a single time point across sites, which cannot detect a shifted trajectory if curves cross. Delay may be large in timing but small in magnitude at any one age. Single-site longitudinal studies also have selection bias, which the 2026 review flags.
next_step: Add the 2026 longitudinal review as the current summary of trajectory studies and note its null pooled grey-matter result; distinguish 'delayed timing' from 'smaller differences at a single scan' in plain language.

topic: White-matter (DTI) differences: robust or fragile?
claim: Lower FA in the corpus callosum in pooled studies is fragile: not in children analysed alone, null in high-quality studies, and possibly due to head motion.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: The largest review (129 studies) found the high-quality-only analysis null and no effect in children; a meta-analysis showed most motion-matched studies found no FA difference.

sources.citation: Parlatini V, et al. White matter alterations in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a systematic review of 129 diffusion imaging studies with meta-analysis. Mol Psychiatry. 2023.
Aoki Y, et al. Research Review: Diffusion tensor imaging studies of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: meta-analyses and reflections on head motion. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2018.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A mega-analysis of raw DTI from 6,993 youths aged 6-18 in five cohorts found ADHD associated with lower FA in the inferior longitudinal and left uncinate fasciculi (largest d -0.3), specific to ADHD versus mood/anxiety/externalising problems, and holding after matching on in-scanner motion.

sources.citation: Sudre G, et al. A mega-analytic study of white matter microstructural differences across 5 cohorts of youths with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Biol Psychiatry. 2023.

why_they_may_differ: Literature meta-analyses pool small studies with varied scanners and tract definitions; the mega-analysis harmonised raw data and controlled motion, giving power to detect small effects. The tracts also differ (corpus callosum in meta-analyses versus inferior longitudinal/uncinate in the mega-analysis), so 'fragile' may apply to the callosal finding but not to white-matter differences in children generally.
next_step: Add Sudre 2023 to the white-matter section and the summary table; revise 'not robust in children' to say a motion-matched mega-analysis in children found small differences in different tracts.

topic: Dopamine transporter: lower or higher in ADHD?
claim: Dopamine scans disagree on direction: lower DAT in never-medicated adults (Volkow) versus 14% higher pooled striatal DAT (Fusar-Poli), with the medication explanation disputed.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Never-medicated adults show lower DAT (and D2/D3) availability in reward regions; a 2024 SPECT study of 20 drug-naive adults also found lower DAT in the nucleus accumbens, with inattention linked to lower caudate DAT.

sources.citation: Volkow ND, et al. Evaluating dopamine reward pathway in ADHD: clinical implications. JAMA. 2009.
Itagaki S, et al. Reduced dopamine transporter availability in drug-naive adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. PCN Rep. 2024.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Pooled across 9 PET/SPECT studies, striatal DAT was on average 14% higher in ADHD, higher in previously medicated and lower in drug-naive samples, suggesting upregulation as an adaptation to stimulants; a letter disputed the medication coding.

sources.citation: Fusar-Poli P, et al. Striatal dopamine transporter alterations in ADHD: pathophysiology or adaptation to psychostimulants? A meta-analysis. Am J Psychiatry. 2012.
Spencer TJ, et al. Striatal dopamine transporter binding in adults with ADHD. Am J Psychiatry. 2012.

why_they_may_differ: Tracers differ in selectivity (e.g., beta-CIT also binds serotonin transporters), regions differ (whole striatum versus accumbens), samples are tiny, and prior medication may up-regulate DAT. The newer drug-naive study fits Fusar-Poli's own suggestion that drug-naive samples show lower DAT, so the medication-adaptation explanation and the 'lower in untreated ADHD' finding are compatible. No pooled analysis since 2012 was found.
next_step: Add Itagaki 2024 as a further drug-naive data point; note tracer differences in the table; search for any post-2012 DAT meta-analysis or longitudinal PET before/after stimulant exposure to test the adaptation hypothesis directly.

topic: Is hyperfocus more common in diagnosed ADHD?
claim: People with more ADHD symptoms report hyperfocus more often; there are 'no studies of how common it is in diagnosed adults'.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: In online adult samples (pilot n = 251, replication n = 372), higher ADHD symptoms went with more frequent hyperfocus in school, hobbies and screen time; a 12-item dispositional scale correlated r = 0.53 with an ADHD rating scale.

sources.citation: Hupfeld KE, et al. Living "in the zone": hyperfocus in adult ADHD. Atten Defic Hyperact Disord. 2019.
Hupfeld KE, et al. Validation of the dispositional adult hyperfocus questionnaire (AHQ-D). Sci Rep. 2024.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: In a study that included 78 diagnosed adults compared with matched controls, patients and controls did not differ in occurrence, frequency, duration or pervasiveness of hyperfocus (hyperfocus was less likely in educational and social settings in ADHD), although ADHD traits correlated with hyperfocus frequency in 1,124 healthy adults. The authors concluded hyperfocus is not specific to ADHD patients.

sources.citation: Groen Y, et al. Testing the relation between ADHD and hyperfocus experiences. Res Dev Disabil. 2020.

why_they_may_differ: Trait correlations in online community samples can arise from shared self-report style (people endorsing many experiences), while a diagnosed clinical group compared with matched controls tests the clinical claim directly. Questionnaires differ, and 'hyperfocus' has no agreed definition.
next_step: Add Groen 2020 to the page and remove or revise 'no studies of how common it is in diagnosed adults'; the page already says hyperfocus is not unique to ADHD, which Groen supports more strongly than the current sources.

topic: Is emotion dysregulation a core part of ADHD?
claim: Emotion dysregulation is common but not a listed symptom; experts disagree whether it should be (core, separate-but-related, or a subgroup).

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Emotional impulsivity and deficient emotional self-regulation may be specific enough to ADHD to serve as diagnostic criteria; a 2026 meta-analysis of 75 studies (63 on ADHD) found emotion dysregulation correlated with externalising symptoms (r = 0.35; lability r = 0.47) regardless of age, sex, informant, subtype, comorbidity or medication.

sources.citation: Faraone SV, et al. Practitioner Review: Emotional dysregulation in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder - implications for clinical recognition and intervention. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2019.
Njardvik U, et al. Emotion dysregulation in children and adolescents with externalizing disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2026.
Soler-Gutiérrez AM, et al. Evidence of emotion dysregulation as a core symptom of adult ADHD: a systematic review. PLoS One. 2023.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Emotion dysregulation affects only a portion of children with ADHD in clinic studies and is best seen as a dimension; competing models treat it as a separate correlated problem or the mark of a subgroup; emotional symptoms are non-specific across disorders and there is no agreed definition.

sources.citation: Shaw P, et al. Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Am J Psychiatry. 2014.

why_they_may_differ: A moderate correlation (r about 0.35) means emotion dysregulation travels with ADHD symptoms but is far from identical to them, which each camp reads differently. Much of the adult evidence is self-report, and overlap with mood, anxiety and trauma conditions makes specificity hard to test. The definitional problem (lability, irritability, emotional impulsivity) is acknowledged by both sides.
next_step: Add the 2026 meta-analysis (r = 0.35, lability 0.47) as the best current estimate of strength of association in young people; note Faraone 2019 as the 'core symptom' side so the debate has a named source on each side.

topic: Executive deficits: a subgroup or nearly everyone?
claim: Executive weaknesses are 'neither necessary nor sufficient'; older estimates put executive impairment at a third to a half of children with ADHD, while one study found 89%.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Medium average effects with heavy overlap mean many people with ADHD test in the normal range; executive deficit may mark only a subgroup (roughly a third to a half).

sources.citation: Willcutt EG, et al. Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biol Psychiatry. 2005.
Nigg JT, et al. Causal heterogeneity in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: do we need neuropsychologically impaired subtypes? Biol Psychiatry. 2005.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Using several tests per skill and latent modelling to remove test unreliability, 89% of children with ADHD were impaired on at least one executive domain (working memory 62%).

sources.citation: Kofler MJ, et al. Executive functioning heterogeneity in pediatric ADHD. J Abnorm Child Psychol. 2019.

why_they_may_differ: Single tests are unreliable and capture one skill, so they under-detect impairment; aggregating multiple tests raises detection but also the chance of finding 'impairment' in one of several domains (the 89% is 'any of three'), and the comparison-group impairment rate matters. The cut-off for 'impaired' varies.
next_step: Find the comparison-group rate of 'impaired on at least one domain' in Kofler 2019 so the 89% can be read against a baseline; look for a replication of multi-indicator estimates in a larger or adult sample.

topic: Does poor sleep cause ADHD, or the reverse?
claim: Which causes which is not settled; research is mostly cross-sectional and cannot tell the directions apart.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: A bidirectional Mendelian randomisation study (genetic variants as natural experiments) estimated that genetically predicted insomnia raised ADHD risk (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.22-1.45), with a suggestive link from ADHD to shorter sleep.

sources.citation: Sun X, et al. Sleep disturbance and psychiatric disorders: a bidirectional Mendelian randomisation study. Epidemiol Psychiatr Sci. 2022.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: An earlier Mendelian randomisation study found insomnia causally linked to autism and bipolar disorder, but no significant causal estimate in either direction for ADHD.

sources.citation: Gao X, et al. The bidirectional causal relationships of insomnia with five major psychiatric disorders: a Mendelian randomization study. Eur Psychiatry. 2019.

why_they_may_differ: Different insomnia GWAS instruments, different (older versus newer) ADHD GWAS, and different pleiotropy filters (HEIDI versus multiple robust estimators). Insomnia variants overlap with general psychiatric liability, which can mimic causation. MR estimates lifelong genetic tendency, not the effect of a bad night or of treating sleep.
next_step: Add a sentence that genetic (Mendelian randomisation) studies exist and disagree; check for newer MR using the 2023 ADHD GWAS and for prospective cohort studies testing whether early sleep problems predict later ADHD symptoms.

topic: Do menopausal symptoms differ in women with ADHD?
claim: Two 2025 menopause studies comparing women with and without ADHD disagreed: Iceland found more perimenopausal symptoms, a UK survey found no difference by diagnosis.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Women with ADHD report more menopausal symptoms: in Iceland, severe perimenopausal symptoms in 54% with ADHD against 30% without; an Irish 2026 survey of 602 women (377 with self-reported ADHD) also found greater menopausal symptom severity.

sources.citation: Jakobsdóttir Smári U, et al. Perimenopausal symptoms in women with and without ADHD: a population-based cohort study. Eur Psychiatry. 2025.
Boyd C, et al. ADHD and the female reproductive stages: menstruation, perinatal and menopause. Arch Womens Ment Health. 2026.
sources.design: cross-sectional online survey with comparison group

positions.label: B
positions.summary: In 656 UK women aged 45-60, a diagnosis of ADHD was not linked to worse menopausal symptoms at any stage, although more ADHD traits were linked to more complaints.

sources.citation: Chapman L, et al. Examining the link between ADHD symptoms and menopausal experiences. J Atten Disord. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: All are cross-sectional self-report studies with self-reported diagnosis. The UK study excluded hormone-therapy and pill users (who may be the most symptomatic) and recruited women 45-60; Iceland's sample was younger (35-55) and found the largest gap at 35-39, before most women's transition; the Irish survey recruited partly via ADHD support groups, which may select more symptomatic women. Trait-based analyses in the UK study point the same direction as the other two, so the disagreement may be about diagnosis versus traits more than about whether a link exists.
next_step: Add Boyd 2026 as a third comparison study (noting its support-group recruitment), so the balance is visible as two-to-one on diagnosis with all three agreeing on traits. Watch for any longitudinal study through the menopause transition, which would settle whether symptoms change rather than differ.

topic: Hormonal contraception and mood in ADHD
claim: The effects of hormonal contraception and hormone therapy on ADHD have not been studied well enough to summarise.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: The page treats hormonal contraception as unstudied in ADHD.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A Swedish register study of 29,767 young women with ADHD aged 15-24 and 763,146 without found women with ADHD had higher depression risk overall, and a larger excess when using oral hormonal contraception (combined pill hazard ratio 5.19 against non-users without ADHD).

sources.citation: Lundin C, et al. Hormonal Contraceptive Use and Risk of Depression Among Young Women With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2023.

why_they_may_differ: The page's statement is about effects on ADHD symptoms, which remain unstudied; the registry addresses depression during contraceptive use. It is observational, so women prescribed the pill may differ from non-users, and depression diagnoses in records may reflect contact with services. Relative figures need absolute rates added.
next_step: Revise the bullet to say that effects on ADHD symptoms are unstudied, but a large Swedish registry found higher depression risk in young women with ADHD using oral contraception; obtain absolute depression rates from the full text before quoting, and frame contraception choices as decisions with a clinician.

topic: Recalled versus measured symptom change across hormonal stages; strength of expert claims
claim: An expert review states hormonal transitions worsen ADHD symptoms and mood; the systematic review calls evidence 'largely suggestive'; a 2026 survey found large recalled worsening but similar measured severity across stages.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Hormonal transitions worsen ADHD: the Eunethydis expert review states this, and most women in surveys recall worsening (98% around menopause, 89% across the cycle). A 2026 three-group study found women with ADHD more often screened positive for PMDD than women without ADHD.

sources.citation: Kooij JJS, et al. Research advances and future directions in female ADHD: the lifelong interplay of hormonal fluctuations with mood, cognition, and disease. Front Glob Womens Health. 2025.
Groenman AP, et al. The monthly spectrum: Premenstrual symptoms across ADHD and autism. Womens Health (Lond). 2026.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: The best syntheses and measured data are weaker: the systematic review found 11 mostly small studies and 'largely suggestive' evidence, and when current symptoms were scored with a standard questionnaire, severity was similar across life stages despite recalled worsening.

sources.citation: Osianlis E, et al. ADHD and sex hormones in females: a systematic review. J Atten Disord. 2025.
Osianlis E, et al. ADHD in females: survey findings on symptoms across hormonal life stages. J Psychiatr Res. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: Recall of change is shaped by expectation and by the worst periods, while a single current-symptom score cannot capture within-person change across stages; neither design follows the same women through a transition. The expert review draws on clinical experience and women's accounts, which are valuable for generating hypotheses but go beyond the systematic evidence. The PMDD finding concerns premenstrual mood, not ADHD core symptoms.
next_step: Page handles this well. Optionally add Groenman 2026 as the first PMDD study with a non-ADHD comparison group (strengthening the cycle-mood point while noting small numbers). Prioritise any prospective daily-tracking study when it appears.

topic: How many children still have ADHD as adults
claim: About 15% still meet full criteria at 25 and about 65% if partial remission is counted (Faraone 2006); about 90% of the MTA cohort still had some symptoms.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Low persistence on strict criteria: 15% at full criteria in the 2006 meta-analysis; in population cohorts, 21.9% of children with ADHD in England (E-Risk) and 17.2% in Brazil (Pelotas) still met criteria at 18-19, and 3 of 61 in Dunedin at 38.

sources.citation: Faraone SV, et al. The age-dependent decline of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis of follow-up studies. Psychol Med. 2006.
Agnew-Blais JC, et al. Evaluation of the Persistence, Remission, and Emergence of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Young Adulthood. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.
Caye A, et al. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Trajectories From Childhood to Young Adulthood: Evidence From a Birth Cohort Supporting a Late-Onset Syndrome. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: High persistence in clinical cohorts with repeated, multi-informant assessment: in the MTA, combining parent and self-reports, 60% showed symptom persistence and 41% met symptom and impairment criteria in young adulthood, and about 90% had residual symptoms over the whole follow-up.

sources.citation: Sibley MH, et al. Defining ADHD symptom persistence in adulthood: optimizing sensitivity and specificity. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2017.
sources.design: clinical cohort (MTA), comparison of persistence definitions

sources.citation: Sibley MH, et al. Variable patterns of remission from ADHD in the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD. Am J Psychiatry. 2022.

why_they_may_differ: Persistence depends on who reports (self-reports by young adults give much lower rates than parent reports), the threshold (DSM's six symptoms, which were written for children, versus age-adjusted norms), whether impairment is required, and the sample (clinic-referred, more severe children in MTA versus community cases, some milder, in birth cohorts). Single snapshots also miss people who are between episodes.
next_step: The page handles the definitional point well. Add the informant effect (Sibley 2017: parent versus self-report) to the existing 'self-report versus others' report' bullet with a citation, and cite at least one population cohort (E-Risk or Pelotas) so the low-persistence end does not rest on a 2006 meta-analysis and Dunedin alone. Mirror any change on 01-is-this-real/diagnosed-as-an-adult.md, which repeats the 15%/65% figures.

topic: Adult-onset ADHD
claim: Adult onset is contested; the usual view now is that most 'late' ADHD began in adolescence or was missed, with true adult onset unresolved.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Three population birth cohorts found most young-adult or adult ADHD had no childhood diagnosis: 90% in Dunedin (age 38), 67.5% in E-Risk (age 18) and 87.4% in Pelotas (age 18-19), and the Pelotas authors proposed two distinct syndromes.

sources.citation: Moffitt TE, et al. Is adult ADHD a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder? Evidence from a four-decade longitudinal cohort study. Am J Psychiatry. 2015.
Agnew-Blais JC, et al. Evaluation of the Persistence, Remission, and Emergence of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Young Adulthood. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.
Caye A, et al. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Trajectories From Childhood to Young Adulthood: Evidence From a Birth Cohort Supporting a Late-Onset Syndrome. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Careful, repeated assessment shrinks late onset: in the MTA about 95% of apparent late-onset cases were excluded; in a later Pelotas follow-up at 22, latent-trajectory analysis found 78% of adults with ADHD had persistent symptoms from childhood and 67% a neurodevelopmental course, with the remainder rising after puberty.

sources.citation: Sibley MH, et al. Late-onset ADHD reconsidered with comprehensive repeated assessments between ages 10 and 25. Am J Psychiatry. 2018.
sources.design: clinical cohort (MTA local normative comparison group)

sources.citation: Breda V, et al. The neurodevelopmental nature of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults. Br J Psychiatry. 2021.

why_they_may_differ: Birth cohorts used brief childhood assessments (and in some cases few informants), so subthreshold or missed childhood ADHD looks like 'new' adult ADHD; adult diagnoses were often made without excluding substance use, depression or anxiety. The MTA reassessment used full clinical evaluation and multiple informants but studied a smaller comparison group. Breda's reanalysis of the same Pelotas cohort reached a more continuous picture using symptom trajectories rather than diagnostic cut-offs, showing the definition largely drives the answer.
next_step: Cite E-Risk and Pelotas alongside Dunedin, since three independent cohorts carry more weight than one, and add Breda 2021 to show the Pelotas team's own later, more continuous finding. Check that 01-is-this-real/diagnosed-as-an-adult.md frames the debate the same way.

topic: Life expectancy: counted versus modelled
claim: The '13 years' figure is a calculator estimate; a UK study that counted deaths found life expectancy 6.8 (men) and 8.6 (women) years shorter in diagnosed adults, probably more than for everyone with ADHD.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Counted from deaths in UK primary-care records of 30,039 diagnosed adults: 6.8 and 8.6 years less life expectancy, which the authors say probably overstates the gap for all people with ADHD.

sources.citation: O'Nions E, et al. Life expectancy and years of life lost for adults with diagnosed ADHD in the UK: matched cohort study. Br J Psychiatry. 2025.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Modelled with an actuarial calculator from risk-factor answers in a Milwaukee clinical cohort, with no deaths counted: 8.4 fewer total years for the childhood group and about 12.7 years (healthy life) for those whose ADHD persisted.

sources.citation: Barkley RA, et al. Hyperactive child syndrome and estimated life expectancy at young adult follow-up: the role of ADHD persistence and other potential predictors. J Atten Disord. 2019.

why_they_may_differ: One counts actual deaths in diagnosed adults (who are more severely affected than the wider ADHD population, and whose deaths may reflect co-occurring conditions); the other predicts lifespan from present-day risk factors in a small, severe, mostly male clinic sample. Calculators assume risk factors persist and add up, which may not hold. Neither represents undiagnosed adults. Several published commentaries on the UK paper and an author reply exist (Br J Psychiatry 2025-26, e.g. PMIDs 40685928, 40904184, 40910173, 41178080) but have no abstracts, so their arguments were not checked.
next_step: Page handles this carefully and follows safe messaging. Read the UK commentaries and author reply in full; if they raise substantive critiques (for example about matching, coding of ADHD in GP records, or life-table methods), add one line to the 'what is uncertain' section.

topic: Size of the raised risk of suicide death
claim: Suicide deaths: odds ratio 6.7 in a 2019 meta-analysis (four datasets, interval 3.24-17.39); the 2026 meta-analysis found death from suicide about 90% higher.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: A 2019 meta-analysis pooled four datasets and found about 6.7 times the odds of suicide death, with very wide uncertainty.

sources.citation: Septier M, et al. Association between suicidal spectrum behaviors and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2019.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 19 studies (about 16 million people) found a hazard ratio of roughly 1.9 for suicide death, a much smaller relative increase.

sources.citation: Corrigan L, et al. Mortality among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Netw Open. 2026.

why_they_may_differ: The 2019 estimate rests on four datasets and mixes odds ratios from case-control and cohort designs, which inflate when outcomes are rare and samples are selected; the 2026 estimate pools more and larger cohort studies with hazard ratios and is more precise. Different adjustment for co-occurring depression and substance use, and different eras, also matter. The page gives both numbers in separate paragraphs without saying they disagree or which is more reliable.
next_step: In the suicide paragraph, state that the larger, newer meta-analysis gives a smaller relative increase (about 1.9) and that the 6.7 figure rests on four datasets; lead with the more reliable figure. Keep absolute framing ('raised, and still uncommon') and the crisis-contacts link; avoid any method detail, per safe-messaging guidance. Seek an absolute suicide-death rate per 10,000 from a registry source (for example the Danish cohort's cause-specific data).

topic: Smoking in pregnancy
claim: The smoking-in-pregnancy link with ADHD largely disappears when siblings are compared, so it is mostly about families.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Sibling and negative-control designs find the association is explained by family factors: the Swedish sibling estimate was about 0.85, and a three-cohort triangulation study using fathers' smoking as a control and genetic scores found no causal intrauterine effect.

sources.citation: Skoglund C, et al. Familial confounding of the association between maternal smoking during pregnancy and ADHD in offspring. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2014.
sources.design: registry with sibling and cousin comparisons

sources.citation: Haan E, et al. Prenatal smoking, alcohol and caffeine exposure and maternal-reported attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms in childhood: triangulation of evidence using negative control and polygenic risk score analyses. Addiction. 2022.
sources.design: negative-control (paternal) and polygenic score triangulation across ALSPAC, Generation R and MoBa
sources.n: up to about 42,000 children per cohort

sources.citation: Tsegay L, et al. Maternal and paternal smoking during pregnancy and the risk of ADHD in offspring: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. J Psychiatr Res. 2026.
sources.n: 6 meta-analyses; about 2.2 million participants for maternal smoking

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Pooled observational studies consistently find raised odds (about 1.7 for maternal smoking), and a 2024 two-sample Mendelian randomisation study reported a causal effect (odds ratio 2.54), though a published comment judged that evidence inconclusive.

sources.citation: Xie T, et al. The causal impact of maternal smoking around birth on offspring ADHD: A two-sample Mendelian randomization study. J Affect Disord. 2024.
Sorjonen K, et al. Inconclusive evidence for a causal impact of maternal smoking on offspring ADHD in a Mendelian randomization study by Xie and Mao (2024). J Affect Disord. 2024.

why_they_may_differ: Whole-population studies cannot separate smoking from the mother's own ADHD-linked genes and circumstances. The umbrella review found fathers' smoking was linked to ADHD almost as strongly as mothers', which is hard to explain by a direct effect in the womb and points to family confounding. The Mendelian randomisation study used variants for the mother's smoking measured in adults' own genomes ('maternal smoking around birth' as reported by UK Biobank participants), which also partly measure the child's inherited liability, so it may not isolate the pregnancy exposure; its critics made this kind of point.
next_step: Keep the page's conclusion but strengthen it with the paternal-smoking negative control (Tsegay 2026, Haan 2022), which is easier for readers to follow than sibling designs. If the Xie MR result is mentioned anywhere on the site, pair it with the critique. Confirm the Skoglund sample size from the full record before quoting it.

topic: Alcohol in pregnancy
claim: Not covered on the page: whether drinking alcohol in pregnancy causes ADHD.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Heavy prenatal alcohol exposure causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), and ADHD is among the most common diagnoses in people with prenatal alcohol exposure; ADHD-like symptoms in FASD can be mistaken for ADHD.

sources.citation: Clark CA, et al. Prevalence of co-occurring diagnoses in people exposed to alcohol prenatally: Findings from a meta-analysis. J Affect Disord. 2024.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: For the light-to-moderate drinking that most pregnant drinkers report, sibling and negative-control designs find at most a very weak link with ADHD symptoms and none with an ADHD diagnosis.

sources.citation: Eilertsen EM, et al. Maternal alcohol use during pregnancy and offspring attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a prospective sibling control study. Int J Epidemiol. 2017.
sources.design: prospective cohort with sibling control and negative control (MoBa)

sources.citation: Haan E, et al. Prenatal smoking, alcohol and caffeine exposure and maternal-reported attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms in childhood: triangulation of evidence using negative control and polygenic risk score analyses. Addiction. 2022.
sources.design: negative-control and polygenic score triangulation, three cohorts
sources.n: up to about 42,000 children per cohort

why_they_may_differ: The two sides concern different doses. Heavy or binge exposure has well-established effects on the developing brain; the cohort studies mostly capture low, self-reported drinking, where familial confounding dominates and true effects, if any, are small. Self-report of drinking in pregnancy is also under-reported, which biases towards no effect.
next_step: Add a short alcohol paragraph to the causes page (a common parental worry), separating heavy exposure and FASD from light drinking, and link to any FASD differential-diagnosis content on is-it-adhd-or-something-else. Avoid wording that implies drinking in pregnancy is safe; national guidance advises none.

topic: Very preterm birth: does the link survive sibling comparison?
claim: Very preterm birth is consistently linked to ADHD (odds ratio 3.04) but cause is not established; whether it holds in sibling comparisons was not checked for this page.

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Meta-analysis of 12 studies: very or extremely preterm or very low birth weight children have about three times the odds of ADHD; the page treats causation as open.

sources.citation: Franz AP, et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and very preterm/very low birth weight: a meta-analysis. Pediatrics. 2018.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Sibling designs show the link largely survives: in Norway, early-preterm children scored about 0.24 SD higher on ADHD symptoms after accounting for family factors, and a systematic review of 140 twin and sibling studies listed low birth weight and gestational age among the few early factors still linked to ADHD after familial adjustment.

sources.citation: Ask H, et al. Association of Gestational Age at Birth With Symptoms of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children. JAMA Pediatr. 2018.
Carlsson T, et al. Early environmental risk factors for neurodevelopmental disorders - a systematic review of twin and sibling studies. Dev Psychopathol. 2021.
sources.design: systematic review of twin and sibling studies

why_they_may_differ: This is less a contradiction than a gap the page itself flags. The meta-analysis pooled ordinary comparisons; the sibling studies remove shared family factors and still find a link, which makes a causal contribution of very early birth more plausible than for smoking or paracetamol. Sibling effects were modest (around a quarter of a standard deviation) and stronger for inattention.
next_step: Replace 'whether this holds in sibling comparisons was not checked' with the Ask 2018 and Carlsson 2021 findings, and adjust the short answer: preterm birth is the one exposure on the page whose link survives sibling comparison. Look for absolute ADHD rates by gestational age in a registry source to meet the absolute-risk rule.

topic: Screens and ADHD symptoms
claim: Screens are linked with later ADHD symptoms, but cause is unproven (based on one US cohort of 2,587 teenagers).

positions.label: A
positions.summary: Some longitudinal and genetic studies suggest digital media may raise later ADHD symptoms: the US cohort found 9.5% against 4.6%; a review of 28 longitudinal studies found effects in both directions, more consistent for problematic use; one Mendelian randomisation study reported that genetically predicted phone and TV time raised childhood ADHD risk.

sources.citation: Ra CK, et al. Association of digital media use with subsequent symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder among adolescents. JAMA. 2018.
Thorell LB, et al. Longitudinal associations between digital media use and ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents: a systematic literature review. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2024.
Meng Z, et al. Relationships between screen time and childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a Mendelian randomization study. Front Psychiatry. 2024.

positions.label: B
positions.summary: Other designs find the link is small or largely genetic: a meta-analysis of 87 studies found only a small correlation of screen time with behaviour problems (r 0.11); in 4,262 US children, shared genetic risk accounted for most or all of the screen time-attention link; and a second Mendelian randomisation study found genetically predicted leisure screen time associated with lower ADHD risk.

sources.citation: Eirich R, et al. Association of Screen Time With Internalizing and Externalizing Behavior Problems in Children 12 Years or Younger: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2022.
Zhang Y, et al. Shared Genetic Risk in the Association of Screen Time With Psychiatric Problems in Children. JAMA Netw Open. 2023.
Cai C, et al. Leisure Screen Time and the Risk of Six Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Two-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study. Brain Behav. 2025.

why_they_may_differ: Screen time is self- or parent-reported and bundled with sleep, family conflict and genes that also shape attention. Polygenic designs suggest the same inherited tendencies drive both, while the two Mendelian randomisation studies, using adult screen-time variants from the same UK Biobank-type data, reached opposite conclusions, which suggests the genetic instruments are not specific to screen use. Reciprocal effects mean children with attention problems may drift towards heavier or more problematic use.
next_step: Replace or supplement the single 2018 cohort with the Eirich meta-analysis (small effect) and Thorell review (reciprocal effects), and mention genetic confounding (Zhang 2023). Do not cite either MR study alone; if cited, cite both as showing the method gives contradictory answers here.

topic: Does childhood ADHD medication protect against later substance problems?
claim: Prescribed medication has not been found to raise later addiction risk; in observational studies medicated periods had fewer substance-related problems ('if anything, medicated periods are associated with fewer substance problems').

positions.label: A
